candidates.title: Towards guideline-grounded clinical decision-making: a multi-scale study of retrieval augmented generation based large language model agents
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) show promise for clinical decision support but are limited by opaque knowledge and inconsistent decision-making. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates these issues by injecting verifiable passages from a curated corpus at inference time. Using 2,400 real patient pathways from the MIMIC-CDM dataset, we evaluated RAG configurations over information gathering, diagnostic accuracy, treatment recommendations and guideline retrieval, identifying key factors for integrating RAG into clinical AI-agents. Across eight general and medical LLMs spanning 1B to 70B parameters, RAG consistently increased mean diagnostic accuracy from 55.64% to 64.29%, an 8.65-points gain (P=0.0039). In a matched three-backbone analysis, RAG improved physical-examination, imaging and laboratory clinician test-ordering alignment by 5.17 points and treatment alignment by 3.97 points, while surfacing verifiable guideline citations for clinicians. Benefits depended on retrieval design, with autonomous query rewriting producing the clearest effect on retrieval fidelity and downstream performance. These findings demonstrate that guideline-grounded RAG can improve both the outcomes and clinical-decision pathways of LLM-agents while increasing their traceability and transparency.

candidates.title: Scaling the Expert Eye: Automating Subsurface Model Evaluation and Tuning via Reservoir Engineering Inspired AI Agents
candidates.abstract: Abstract Predicting the behavior of oil fields is a notoriously complex endeavor, often relying on high-fidelity predictive models (e.g. simulation models) that are sensitive to a myriad of geological and operational parameters. Traditionally, the "gold standard" for refining these models has been the manual intervention by reservoir engineers. These experts possess the nuanced domain knowledge required to interpret data anomalies and perform "history matching"—adjusting model inputs to align with historical performance. However, this human-centric approach is often a bottleneck; it is slow, difficult to scale, and limited by the speed at which a human can iterate through high-dimensional data sets. To address this, we introduce an autonomous AI agent designed to bridge the gap between expert intuition and computational efficiency. In order to perform this task autonomously, the AI Agent needs the ability to do the following: (1) Validate a model's quality using the same qualitative and quantitative metrics as used by the experts (2) Determine what needs to be changed and how to change them to improve the model (3) Modify these parameters and evaluate the model in order to improve the model (4) Repeat the process until all metrics are satisfied. This is achieved by using state-of-the-art LLMs (large language models) with system prompts fed with documentation of all the steps above, along with LangChain-based agent architecture developed specifically for this purpose. By codifying the analytical workflows and heuristic strategies used by veteran reservoir engineers, the agent performs automated parameter tuning across predictive models. The system leverages an assisted data assimilation approach already in place, using rigorous back-testing to evaluate the impact of each adjustment in real-time. Instead of a brute-force search, the agent applies specialized logic to identify which "knobs" to turn—such as permeability or porosity ranges —to generate results that best mirror reality, effectively mimicking the "expert eye" at scale. The integration of this agent transforms the modeling pipeline from a labor-intensive manual task into a high-speed, expert-driven optimization process. Initial results tested on multiple real field models demonstrate that the agent can achieve model fidelity comparable to manual tuning while significantly reducing the time-to-insight from weeks to hours, and also minimizing critical errors that might be introduced by human engineers due to the complex model validation process. By automating the iterative back-testing/history-matching cycle, organizations can democratize the specialized knowledge of their top engineers across entire portfolios of assets. This ensures that predictive models remain robust, reliable, and grounded in the practical realities of field operations, allowing human engineers to focus on high-level strategic decision-making rather than repetitive parameter tweaking.

candidates.title: Mapping the Silence: Cross-Lingual Asymmetries in Large Language Model Refusal and Evasion on Sensitive History
candidates.abstract: As large language models increasingly shape public discourse, this study evaluates how US and China-based models govern access to politically sensitive history in US English and Mandarin Chinese. Across 2,400 interactions covering sixty globally significant events, we examined how prompt configurations modulate LLM responses. Chinese models demonstrated statistically significant cross-lingual disparities, restricting Mandarin queries up to three times more than English queries. Furthermore, models were substantially more likely to restrict responses to subjective, political, or contemporary framings than factual queries, highlighting the need for further evaluation of cross-lingual differences in AI systems and their security implications in politically sensitive contexts.

candidates.title: From General-Purpose Large Language Models to Domain-Specific Financial Models: A Structured Review and Comparative Case Analysis
candidates.abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) in finance has expanded rapidly, yet general-purpose systems face recurring problems in high-risk and regulated applications: Unsupported factual generation, weak reasoning across text, tables, charts, and numerical data, and limited traceability of model-assisted decisions. This study conducts a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta Analyses (PRISMA)-informed structured review of 67 studies, principally published between January 2020 and March 2026, with three foundational pre-2020 studies retained through backward citation tracking. It develops a qualitative analytical and diagnostic framework with three pathways: Specialized knowledge modeling, task-constrained multimodal reasoning, and Trust-by-Design. A study-level evidence map and an explicit coding protocol show how the pathways were derived. The framework is used to compare BloombergGPT, FinGPT, FinTral, Fin-o1, Fin-R1, and Agentar-Fin-R1 through common criteria for knowledge controls, modality handling, lifecycle governance, evidence quality, and deployment maturity. The case analysis distinguishes model-paper design descriptions, developer reported benchmark results, platform-level deployment reports, and prospective applications. The analysis indicates that financial LLMs differ materially in how they organize domain knowledge, coordinate heterogeneous inputs, and govern model use across the lifecycle. Agentar-Fin-R1 illustrates the framework; the case does not validate the framework or establish independently observed production performance. The paper provides a structured basis for assessing domain-specific financial LLMs and connects responsible model design with sustainable financial innovation through durable governance arrangements, controlled model and compliance risk, responsible scaling, financial inclusion, and institutional resilience. Received: 1 April 2026 | Revised: 2 September 2026 | Accepted: 20 September 2026 Conflicts of Interest The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest to this work. Data Availability Statement Tables S1–S4 in the Supplementary Materials provide the prospective replication protocol, the study-level evidence map for the 67-study corpus, the code-to-pathway derivation and threshold rationale, and the register of seven sources outside the review corpus. The original query-level exports, source-specific yields, and coder-level screening logs were not retained. Data sharing is not applicable to this article as no new data were created or analyzed in this study. candidates.title: A Large Language Model Framework for Risk Cause Interpretation and Mitigation Recommendation in Drilling Operations
candidates.abstract: Summary When drilling risks such as kick events occur, rapidly identifying the root causes and recommending effective mitigation measures is critical for well control and operational safety. Traditional incident analysis mainly relies on expert experience and rule-based diagnostics, which are time-consuming and often lack systematic interpretability. This paper proposes a Large Language Model (LLM)-based framework to automatically interpret risk causes and generate mitigation recommendations following drilling risk events. Historical drilling incident reports, operational logs, engineering guidelines, and mitigation case records are first collected to construct a drilling risk knowledge base. A word embedding model is then domain-fine-tuned using drilling-related corpora to enhance semantic representation of domain-specific terminology and operational context. Based on the enhanced embeddings, a knowledge retrieval mechanism identifies relevant historical cases and engineering knowledge. The retrieved knowledge and event descriptions—including drilling parameters and operational records—are provided to a Large Language Model, which performs structured reasoning to interpret possible causes and generate recommended mitigation measures. The proposed framework is evaluated using drilling incident datasets covering 45 wells and 56 recorded risk cases from wells drilled in western China oilfields, together with associated drilling reports and operational documentation. Experimental results show that domain-fine-tuned word embeddings significantly improve semantic retrieval performance, increasing relevant case retrieval accuracy from 0.713 to 0.863. With the enhanced knowledge retrieval, the LLM can effectively identify key contributing factors and produce structured explanations of incident causation. The system achieves an overall root-cause interpretation accuracy (RCA-Acc) of 0.864 and generates actionable mitigation recommendations such as adjusting drilling fluid density, optimizing circulation parameters, and strengthening well control monitoring procedures. In addition, the framework provides interpretable reasoning outputs that connect operational conditions, risk indicators, and recommended responses. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly improve the efficiency and consistency of drilling incident analysis while providing practical decision support for field engineers. This study introduces a domain-adapted LLM framework for drilling risk analysis that integrates domain-fine-tuned word embeddings, knowledge retrieval, and large-model reasoning. The proposed approach enables automated cause interpretation and mitigation recommendation after drilling risk events, providing a new paradigm for intelligent incident analysis and decision support in drilling engineering.

candidates.title: A Conversational User Interface for Autonomous Reservoir Simulation Deck Generation and Execution
candidates.abstract: Abstract Objectives/Scope This paper presents CLARISSA (Conversational Language Agent for Reservoir Integrated Simulation System Analysis), a conversational agent that autonomously generates, executes, and analyzes reservoir simulation models from natural language input. Engineers describe what they want; CLARISSA delivers working models. To enable standardized comparison of conversational deck-generation systems, we introduce RIGOR (Reservoir Input Generation Output Review), a benchmark for evaluating CLARISSA and future similar efforts. Methods, Procedures, Process CLARISSA employs large language models integrated with OPM Flow through a multi-stage translation pipeline that converts natural language problem descriptions into PetroScript, a typed, simulator-independent authoring language whose compiler currently emits Eclipse-format deck syntax. The system supports multiple input modalities: voice, text chat, web interfaces, and REST APIs. Physics-aware validation flags inconsistencies during conversational elicitation, while analog databases suggest reasonable defaults for incomplete specifications—all assumptions are explicitly documented. Generated decks execute autonomously on OPM Flow; outputs can be exported for commercial platforms when third-party validation is required. RIGOR employs execution-based evaluation using simulator diagnostics including convergence behavior and material balance closure. Results, Observations, Conclusions CLARISSA successfully generated decks for SPE comparative solution projects including SPE1 (Odeh, 1981), SPE5 (Killough and Kossack, 1987), and SPE9 (Killough, 1995) from text and tabular input specifications. Generated decks executed without error and matched published benchmark results. Beyond validation cases, CLARISSA demonstrated autonomous model reformulation: given only a compositional table, the system converted a black-oil model to a fully compositional equation-of-state formulation without additional user intervention. This capability enables rapid evaluation of tertiary recovery options from existing assets. RIGOR defines complexity tiers from foundational (linear displacement corefloods) through intermediate (multi-well pattern floods) to advanced scenarios requiring mid-conversation compositional pivots. Execution-based scoring derives from simulator diagnostics: convergence behavior, material balance closure, and physical constraint satisfaction. The binding constraint on simulation adoption has never been solver performance—it is human cognitive load and workflow friction. CLARISSA eliminates both commercial licensing barriers and the specialist training traditionally required, enabling practicing reservoir engineers to directly leverage simulation capabilities previously accessible only to dedicated specialists. Novel/Additive Information Unlike prior work focused on querying existing models (SPE-221987) or retrieving reservoir data through pre-built tool functions (SPE-229646), CLARISSA is the first system capable of generating—not merely querying or modifying—complete simulation decks from natural language. RIGOR provides the first standardized benchmark for evaluating conversational deck-generation systems, enabling reproducible comparison of future approaches analogous to established benchmarks in software engineering code generation. PetroScript, to be released alongside RIGOR, is to our knowledge the first typed authoring language for reservoir simulation decks designed to be simulator-independent, replacing positional keyword syntax with named, validated parameters.

candidates.title: Automating Injury Severity Score Calculation From Free-Text Discharge Diagnoses Using Domain-Specific Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models: Retrospective Validation Study
candidates.abstract: Background Trauma registries are crucial for evaluating the prognosis of injuries and the quality of trauma care. However, the calculation of Injury Severity Score (ISS) remains a predominantly manual process, which is labor-intensive, potentially error-prone, and difficult to scale. Automating this process is a critical step toward enhancing the efficiency and quality of trauma registry data. Objective This study conducts a feasibility test on the use of large language models (LLMs) to automatically calculate ISS from free-text discharge diagnoses. We specifically investigate the efficacy of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to enhance LLM accuracy by incorporating knowledge from the Abbreviated Injury Scale. We compare the performance of baseline LLMs against models augmented with both a standard RAG and a novel, domain-specific RAG framework. Methods In this retrospective validation study, we used deidentified, free-text discharge diagnoses from trauma patients at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital (Linkou, Taiwan) in 2022. Against a physician-verified gold standard, we compared the performance of three systems: (1) baseline LLMs, (2) LLMs with standard RAG, and (3) LLMs with domain-specific RAG, for which the retriever was fine-tuned on trauma-related ICD-10 (International Statistical Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision) codes. Performance was evaluated on a physician-verified test set across exact ISS prediction, tolerance-based accuracy, and ISS severity categories. Results Baseline state-of-the-art LLMs achieve modest exact-match (EM) accuracy, ranging from 47.3% to 64.7%. Standard RAG did not produce consistent gains (54.3% to 60.3%), whereas the domain-specific RAG substantially improved accuracy (62.7% to 75.3%). Performance gains were most pronounced in patients with moderate to severe injuries. GPT-4.1 with domain-specific RAG reached the highest EM accuracy (75.3%, 95% CI 66.1%-82.7%), compared with 70.0% for the deterministic International Classification of Diseases and R statistical software (ICDPIC-R) baseline. Tolerance-based and categorical analyses confirm substantial gains with the domain-specific RAG framework in clinically relevant ranges. Conclusions This single-center feasibility study suggests that LLMs augmented with a domain-specific retriever can calculate the ISS from free-text discharge diagnoses with overall accuracy comparable to that of a deterministic coding tool, with the advantage concentrated in the most severe injuries. This approach may help alleviate the administrative burden of manual coding, enhance standardization, and improve the quality of trauma registry data. Future multi-institutional validation is needed to confirm these findings.

candidates.title: Benchmarking the performance of large language models on medical genetics questions: a comparative evaluation of GPT-5.1, Gemini Pro 3, and Claude Opus 4.5
candidates.abstract: Objective This study benchmarks the performance of three state of the art large reasoning models comprising GPT 5.1, Gemini Pro 3, and Claude Opus 4.5 by evaluating their accuracy, response consistency, processing speed, and output length on medical genetics questions from the Turkish Medical Specialty Examination (TUS). Methods A total of 233 medical genetics questions were selected based on predefined inclusion criteria covering molecular mechanisms, inheritance patterns, genetic disorders, and diagnostic techniques. Each question was independently submitted to GPT 5.1, Gemini Pro 3, and Claude Opus 4.5 using a standardized prompt. Model accuracy was compared using McNemar's test. Response consistency was assessed using Cohen's Kappa. Response time and word count were analyzed using the Friedman test with Dunn Bonferroni post hoc comparisons. Results No statistically significant differences were observed in overall accuracy among the models ( p &gt; 0.05). GPT 5.1 achieved the highest accuracy at 97.9 percent followed by Claude Opus 4.5 at 96.6 percent and Gemini Pro 3 at 96.1 percent. Cohen's Kappa indicated moderate qualitative divergence between Gemini Pro 3 and Claude Opus 4.5 with kappa equal to 0.451. Significant differences were found in response time and output length ( p &lt; 0.001). Conclusion Although all models demonstrate similarly high accuracy, they differ in operational behavior, suggesting distinct internal knowledge representations and response strategies.

candidates.title: When Transfer Breaks Fairness: A Group-Conditional Perspective on Fair and Robust Adaptation of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reach users only after a chain of transfer steps: full or parameter-efficient fine-tuning, preference alignment, prompting, and changes to the decoding procedure. Each step alters the model, the distribution it faces, or both. Yet fairness and robustness are usually assessed once, on a single fixed test set. This paper presents a unified group-conditional framework to analyze how transfer affects the fairness and robustness of LLMs, and how existing methods try to preserve these properties. To characterize these trade-offs, we introduce a analytical framework that views fair and robust transfer as constrained distributionally robust optimization. We view fair and robust transfer as constrained distributionally robust optimization whose feasible set is determined by the transfer interface, and we split any change in a fairness gap into an update term, caused by changing the model, and shift term, caused by changing the data. Building on existing fairness-transfer bounds, we record two elementary consequences that the LLM literature has not made explicit: the group-conditional bound on the shift term is tight, and when only one group shifts, the marginal shift equals exactly a \( \pi_{\min} \) fraction of the fairness-relevant shift, where \( \pi_{\min} \) is that group's proportion. We use these observations to classify mitigation methods by interface and by the term they target, to offer a reading under which conflicting findings on low-rank adaptation are compatible, and to derive reporting recommendations. We close with open problems, including per-group certificates, fairness of approximate decoding, and cumulative drift under continual transfer.

candidates.title: MiND: Minimal Deterministic Middleware for Auditable Large Language Model Interactions
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in research software, yet many integrations preserve only the visible prompt and answer while losing structured evidence about configuration, provider metadata, timing, failures, and the exact request procedure. MiND is an open-source, provider-neutral middleware that places a small audit boundary between an application and an LLM. For each attempted interaction it normalizes the input, constructs an explicit request, invokes a provider adapter, normalizes the result, and stores a versioned Cycle Artifact containing the observable execution context. The same core is available through a Python API, command-line interface, local HTTP API, and a self-contained Windows interface. MiND is deliberately non-agentic: it does not infer human intention, expose hidden model reasoning, or claim deterministic repetition of stochastic model output. Its purpose is narrower—to make the surrounding execution procedure inspectable and reusable.

candidates.title: Fair synthetic tabular data generation via disentangled semantic encoding and large language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Synthetic tabular data generation plays a key role in alleviating data scarcity and privacy limitations in machine learning, especially in regulated domains such as finance and healthcare. While many existing methods focus on producing realistic and predictive tabular data, fairness is often not explicitly considered, leading to biased synthetic datasets. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) further enhance data quality through natural language representations, which underscores the need for principled mechanisms that ensure fairness alongside predictive performance. To address this challenge, we propose SENNA, a framework that integrates disentangled semantic representations with LLM-based generation to jointly preserve utility and improve fairness. The framework separates task-relevant and task-independent information in the latent space and leverages these representations to guide generation and validation. Experimental results on three real-world datasets show that SENNA achieves competitive downstream performance, while substantially reducing both group-level disparities and individual-level inequality. We further evaluate the framework across multiple backbones, providing insights into fairness–utility trade-offs in LLM-based tabular data synthesis.

candidates.title: BioAgent-RAG: A Knowledge-Graph-Augmented Multi-Agent LLM Framework with Self-Reflective Verification for Explainable Drug Repurposing
candidates.abstract: Biomedical Knowledge Graphs (KGs) such as PrimeKG and Hetionet offer vast structured repositories for clinical discovery; however, conventional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) suffer from black-box opacity, while standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigms face catastrophic hallucinations and biological implausibility. To resolve this critical trade-off, this paper proposes BioAgent-RAG, a multi-agent orchestrated retrieval-augmented generation framework tailored for complex biomedical reasoning and transparent graph traversal. By integrating autonomous sub-agents for query decomposition, path-based KG grounding, and cross-verification, BioAgent-RAG systematically enhances biological plausibility and reduces reasoning hallucinations. Comprehensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that BioAgent-RAG substantially outperforms existing competitive baselines, RD2-KG, KGiA, and RAG-LLMs. Specifically, on the PrimeKG benchmark, it achieves an ROC-AUC of 0.952, PR-AUC of 0.814, MRR of 0.637, and superior Recall@10 and Recall@50 of 0.715 and 0.868, respectively (p &lt; 0.01). Moreover, evaluated on biological plausibility, BioAgent-RAG yields a Biomedical Factuality Score (BFS) of 0.887 on PrimeKG (0.894 on Hetionet) and a Path Reasoning Score (PRS) of 0.841 (0.862 on Hetionet), demonstrating strong preliminary correlation (0.912) with domain-expert evaluations. These findings suggest that BioAgent-RAG serves as a robust, explainable computational screening tool to prioritize drug repurposing candidates prior to in vitro validation.

candidates.title: Operationalizing Pragmatic Difficulty: Speech Act Hierarchy and the Appropriateness Gap in an AI-Generated Business English Oral Test
candidates.abstract: Large language models can now draft scenario-based test tasks on demand, which raises a validation question that has attracted little attention: does the difficulty of the generated tasks behave as the construct predicts? This study examined an AI-generated oral test of three business speech acts to establish whether the tasks reproduced the theoretically expected ordering of difficulty, where within the rating framework difficulty was located, and whether the ability measured was separable from general business oral proficiency. Thirty business English undergraduates responded to twelve ChatGPT-generated tasks; two trained raters independently scored five performance dimensions, and a simulated BEC oral test supplied an external criterion. Scoring reliability was high (total ICC = .953; Cronbach’s α = .86). A 3 × 5 repeated measures analysis of variance revealed a significant effect of speech act (p = .004, partial η² = .213): apologies were significantly more difficult than requests and refusals, which did not differ from each other. A significant effect of rating dimension (p < .001, partial η² = .237) located the greatest weakness in pragmatic appropriateness and the least in discourse coherence, and a non-significant interaction indicated that this profile held across every act. Test totals correlated strongly but not perfectly with the external criterion (r = .778). The results suggest that construct-informed prompting can produce AI-generated pragmatic tasks with theoretically differentiated difficulty profiles, while pragmatic appropriateness emerged as a relatively stable area of weakness across speech acts.

candidates.title: Comparison of performance of an LLM Council of LFM2.5-1.2B, Qwen3-4B-2507 and Phi-4-Mini- reasoning and Meta LLaMa 3.1 8B against MedGemma 4B on extraction and classification of free-text radiology reports
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated growing potential for clinical natural language processing (NLP) [1–4], including radiological report analysis, while recent studies have explored both domain-specialised medical models and multi-LLM approaches [7,8] for improving reliability and reasoning. However, the comparative performance of LLM Councils and specialised medical LLMs on structured radiological tasks remains underexplored. This study evaluated an LLM Council framework against MedGemma 4B for radiological report analysis. The Council comprised Qwen3-4B-2507, LFM2.5-1.2B, and Phi-4 Mini Reasoning, with LLaMa 3.1 8B as chairman. We hypothesised that MedGemma would outperform the Council due to its specialised medical training. A total of 783 anonymised mammography, hip-knee-ankle (HKA), and brain magnetic resonance (MR) reports from Max Healthcare Saket were analysed for BI-RADS and ACR extraction, pre- versus post-operative HKA classification, and normal versus abnormal brain MR classification. Performance was assessed using accuracy, F1 score, and task-specific metrics. MedGemma achieved higher overall accuracy than the Council (88.72% vs. 83.56%; weighted F1: 0.8653 vs. 0.7389), with significant differences overall (p = 0.0129) and for HKA classification (p = 0.0011), but not mammography or brain MR. However, Qwen3-4B-2507 independently achieved the highest accuracy across all tasks: 91.89% in mammography, 92.93% in HKA, and 90.25% in brain MR, yielding 91.69% overall accuracy and a weighted F1 of 0.8902. Notably, the Council achieved 72.22% HKA accuracy compared with 85.86% for MedGemma. These findings suggest that strong general-purpose reasoning may outperform both consensus-based and specialised approaches for clinical NLP under the conditions evaluated.

candidates.title: Resource-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Compact LLMs for Supply Chain Operations: A Hybrid QLoRA and RAG Approach
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer transformative potential for enterprise automation, particularly within the highly complex and data-dense environments of transportation, supply chain management, and intralogistics. However, deploying foundational models in these specialized domains frequently results in a critical failure mode: confident generative hallucinations regarding company-specific, highly proprietary operational protocols. Furthermore, adapting these massive models typically requires prohibitive computational resources, placing them fundamentally out of reach for regional distribution hubs and mid-sized enterprises constrained by strict hardware budgets. This paper investigates the hypothesis that a compact, instruction-tuned Small Language Model (SLM) can be aggressively fine-tuned and semantically grounded to provide highly accurate, factually bound supply chain support while operating entirely within the constraints of a single commodity GPU. This research presents the end-to-end development, optimization, and deployment of IndustryGPT, a highly specialized logistics LLM. We utilize a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategy, specifically 4-bit Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA), to adapt the 1.1-billion parameter TinyLlama base model using a single 16 GB NVIDIA T4 GPU. To systematically eliminate hallucinations and ground the model in factual warehouse operations, we introduce a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture powered by a local FAISS vector database. This hybrid pipeline dynamically retrieves and injects exact standard operating procedures (SOPs) such as inbound packet scanning workflows, tallying reconciliations, and strict fleet maintenance protocols directly into the inference context window. We evaluate the model's performance on a custom hybrid corpus merging customer support dialogues with synthetic routing data, reporting substantial gains in both structural coherence and factual adherence. The system successfully demonstrates that merging domain-specific supervised fine-tuning with dense vector retrieval allows lightweight, edge-deployed models to achieve enterprise-grade accuracy. Finally, the architecture is deployed via a Gradio web interface, providing an interactive, zero-hallucination conversational agent tailored for localized logistics exception handling, proving that data sovereignty and advanced AI automation can coexist on localized commodity hardware.

candidates.title: An Improved Retrieval-Augmented Generation Agent for UAV Situation Awareness Report Generation
candidates.abstract: Accurate and timely UAV (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) situation awareness is essential for early warning and operational decision-making in low-altitude security, yet the manual analysis of large-scale heterogeneous data is resource-intensive and introduces delays. This study proposes IRAG-UAVSA (Improved Retrieval-Augmented Generation—Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Situation Awareness) Agent, an autonomous situation-awareness report-generation framework based on an improved retrieval-augmented generation architecture. The framework integrates real-time UAV descriptors, including platform type, intent, and threat level, with four task-specific hierarchical knowledge bases. A dual-loop pipeline combines evidence-template-guided hybrid retrieval and cross-encoder reranking with high-level LLM (Large Language Model) reflection, structured evidence filling, rule-based validation, and threshold-triggered iterative retry. A three-level evaluation framework was designed, comprising process-level RAG metrics, automatic natural language evaluation, and human–LLM collaborative scoring. Across 49 domain-screened test inputs, IRAG-UAVSA Agent achieved 93.0% knowledge coverage, 4.1% hallucination, and 91.7% logical consistency, while also obtaining the best SummaC (0.67) and VeriScore (0.83) results among the evaluated baselines. The results indicate that iterative retrieval with explicit evidence constraints can substantially improve the factual grounding, traceability, and practical utility of LLM-generated UAV situation-awareness reports.

candidates.title: Verifier-guided knowledge distillation of large language models for auditable thermal comfort reasoning
candidates.abstract: Occupant-centric building operation requires models that can not only predict thermal sensation, but also justify predictions through auditable reasoning. Traditional mechanistic models, such as Fanger’s predicted mean vote (PMV), often show limited field accuracy, whereas advanced machine learning models can improve prediction but typically remain opaque to facility managers and building operators. This study proposes a verifier-guided knowledge distillation framework for auditable thermal comfort reasoning using a lightweight LLaMA-3.2-3B student model. The framework consists of three sequential stages: (1) knowledge distillation from a teacher model, GPT-4o, to transfer domain-specific explanatory patterns; (2) supervised fine-tuning with ground-truth anchoring and a TSV-weighted loss to improve thermal sensation vote (TSV) prediction while limiting teacher-error propagation; and (3) verifier-guided direct preference optimization using an automated claim-consistency verifier. The verifier extracts factor-direction claims from generated explanations, such as high air temperature or low air speed, and checks them against comfort-centered percentile thresholds derived from the ASHRAE Global Thermal Comfort Database II. On the held-out test split, the final model achieved 42.7 % exact TSV accuracy and 79.9 % ±1 accuracy, comparable to standard tabular baselines on the same split. More importantly, the verifier-guided alignment stage reduced the any-incorrect-claim rate from 52.3 % to 16.5 % and improved linked claim accuracy to 78.3 %. Robustness tests showed reasonable directional consistency under perturbation without strong dependence on PMV or SET proxies. At the hot and cold tails, 81 % of explanations named an HVAC-controllable factor, so compact language models can pair thermal comfort predictions with verifiable, operator-actionable explanations for building operation.

candidates.title: Less can be more for predicting properties with large language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Predicting properties from coordinate–category data—sets of vectors paired with categorical information—is fundamental to computational science, manifesting in materials science as predicting formation energies or elastic moduli from crystal structures. While large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been applied to such tasks, optimal strategies for achieving reliable predictions remain elusive. Here we report fundamental limitations in LLM’s ability to learn from coordinate information in coordinate–category data. Through systematic experiments using synthetic datasets with tunable coordinate and category contributions, and a comprehensive benchmarking framework (MatText), we find that LLMs consistently fail to capture coordinate information while excelling at category patterns. This geometric blindness persists regardless of model size (up to 70 billion parameters), dataset scale (up to 2 × 10 6 structures) or text representation strategy. For material property prediction tasks dominated by structural effects, specialized geometric architectures consistently outperform LLMs, as evidenced by a clear ‘Graph Neural Network Language Model (GNN-LM) wall’ in performance benchmarks. Our analysis provides concrete guidelines for architecture selection in scientific machine learning.

candidates.title: Do large language models keep the hedge? Uncertainty preservation when large language models summarize aviation and maritime incident reports
candidates.abstract: Safety-incident reports are written with deliberate epistemic caution: A reporter marks what was seen, what was inferred, and what remains unsure, and a dropped hedge can turn a tentative observation into an apparent cause. As large language models take over summarizing such reports for triage, indexing, and search, whether they preserve that caution becomes a property of the safety record itself. This study asks whether models keep a reporter's expressed uncertainty when they summarize, testing two hypotheses fixed before any summary was generated: that models systematically harden uncertainty by default and that an explicit instruction to preserve it overcorrects into softening. Six open-weight models summarized 42 real incident reports, 30 from the United States Aviation Safety Reporting System and 12 from the United Kingdom Marine Accident Investigation Branch, under a plain prompt, a preserve prompt, and a paraphrase of it. Uncertainty change was measured two ways: at the passage level, by a deterministic epistemic-marker lexicon, and at the claim level, by aligning those markers between source and summary, each validated against manual annotation and cross-checked against two independent language-model judges. Under plain summarization, all six models hardened the reporter's uncertainty (claim-level hardening 0.59–0.85), dropping explicit hedges almost entirely (retention about 0.08) while epistemic modal verbs survived far better. The preserve instruction reversed the pattern into over-softening: In a cluster-robust logistic regression, it carried an odds ratio of 0.12 (95% CI [0.03, 0.49], p = 0.003) and held once summary length was controlled, so the change reflects expressed certainty rather than compression. In practical terms, the instruction lowered the predicted probability of hardening from about 0.43 to 0.13 (Cohen's h = 0.69), and the effect held in mixed-effects models and under adverse imputation of the missing outputs. The pattern was directionally consistent across the tested models and both instruction wordings. Automated safety triage that relies on model summaries should measure epistemic fidelity directly and not treat a single preserve instruction as a solution.

candidates.title: Benchmarking database-grounded language-model agents for atomistic structure identification
candidates.abstract: Reliable atomistic simulations depend on identifying the coordinates of the intended input structure. Automated frameworks relying on natural-language requests can, however, return plausible coordinates for the wrong phase or isomer. We therefore develop a database-grounded agent that interprets requests, selects records and retrieves coordinates while preserving database provenance. Across ten models, this approach more than doubles the success rate of direct coordinate generation and remains robust across larger sets and repeated calls. Reliable automation should abstain when a request or database does not support a unique choice. We address this by benchmarking selection and abstention together, revealing lower success rates and greater model dependence for this more demanding task. Our open-source implementation is provider-independent, allowing the same procedure to be retained as compatible models evolve. Together, these results establish database grounding, provenance and explicit abstention as complementary requirements for reliable automated access to known atomistic structures.

candidates.title: Smarter Extraction of Scholarly Metadata using Knowledge Graphs, Language Models, and Agents
candidates.abstract: Scholarly metadata is an essential element in the scholarly ecosystem, empowering discovery, interoperability, and provenance and its efficacy relies on metadata quality and coverage. However, with the substantial increase in the number and diversity of research artifacts over time, it has become a cumbersome task to harvest metadata features for scholarly publications, datasets, source code, and machine learning models. These artifacts generate heterogeneous metadata features, which are distributed across various repositories. In addition, large language models (LLMs) and agents have emerged as powerful tools and are now being extensively adopted to facilitate a wide range of tasks across domains, ranging from information extraction to knowledge graphs. Nevertheless, numerous open questions persist regarding their adoption in diversified research disciplines, especially concerning their accuracy, robustness, biases, and societal impact when applied in the context of research metadata, scholarly information extraction, and open science. This workshop aims to cover these exciting aspects centered around metadata features from research artifacts, with a focus on large language models and knowledge graphs.

candidates.title: GaCLLM: Large Language Model with Graph Convolution for Recommendation
candidates.abstract: Leveraging auxiliary textual data can help with user profiling and item characterization in recommender systems (RSs). However, incomplete user and item descriptions limit the potential of textual information. To this end, we propose a graph-aware convolutional large language model (LLM) method, eliciting LLMs to summarize from a high-order interaction graph to generate fine-grained descriptions for users and items. We focus on two challenges in this paper: 1) the incompatibility between structural graph and text-aware LLMs . Although some work converts graph data into textual form using templates and sampling strategies, they limit the LLMs’ ability to maintain a global perspective on graphs for LLM reasoning. 2) the limitation of LLMs’ capability for long context. Simply describing a large-scale graph in a textual format makes LLM struggle to robustly comprehend information from lengthy contextual inputs. To bridge the gap between graph structures and LLMs, we employ the LLM as an aggregator for the graph convolution process, eliciting it to aggregate and refine the graph-based information iteratively. To mitigate the information overload associated with large-scale graphs, we segment the graph processing into manageable steps, progressively incorporating multi-hop information in a least-to-most manner. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

candidates.title: Emergent Languages in Populations of Language Model Agents: From Token Efficiency to Oversight Evasion
candidates.abstract: Monitoring autonomous language model agents currently relies mostly on surface behavior. But what happens when agent populations invent new languages with the goal of avoiding human oversight? Here, we study the emergent languages on Moltbook. For this, we build upon the Moltbook Files dataset and apply a three-stage approach consisting of a rule-based heuristic (about 6000 matches) followed by zero-shot classification (518 kept), and metadata extraction. The resulting categories include token efficiency (166), new natural languages (106), and oversight evasion (59). We conduct both quantitative and qualitative analyses. Our results show that posts proposing new languages for avoiding oversight are judged by DeepSeek-V3.2 as being less aligned than the other categories – and that all languages can be learned by other language models in-context merely from a description of the language. Moreover, manually studying exemplary cases reveals surprisingly sophisticated steganographic protocols like embedding hidden messages in natural language. Although we cannot be certain about the extent of autonomy in ideation of these languages, our results add up to the evidence that monitoring surface behavior may soon be insufficient for retaining control over agent populations.

candidates.title: Distilling Transitional Patterns to Multimodal Large Language Models for Session-based Recommendation
candidates.abstract: Session-based recommendation (SBR) predicts the next item based on anonymous sessions. Traditional SBR explores user intents based on ID collaborations or auxiliary content. To further alleviate data sparsity and cold-start issues, recent Multimodal SBR (MSBR) methods utilize simplistic pre-trained models for modality learning but have limitations in semantic richness. Considering the semantic reasoning abilities of multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) and the practical request for high inference efficiency, we focus on the LLM-enhanced MSBR scenario in this paper, which leverages LLM cognition for comprehensive multimodal representation generation, to enhance downstream MSBR. Tackling this problem faces two challenges: i) how to obtain LLM cognition on both inherent multimodal knowledge and transitional patterns, ii) how to align transitional patterns and inherent knowledge into one unified LLM without increasing inference complexity. To this end, we propose a multimodal LLM-enhanced framework TPAD, which extends a teacher-student distillation paradigm to decouple and align transitional patterns for promoting MSBR. TPAD establishes parallel Knowledge-MLLM and Transfer-MLLM, where the former as student model interprets item knowledge-reflected features and the latter as teacher model extracts transition-aware features. Transitional pattern alignment harnessing mutual information estimation unites two MLLMs, distilling transitional patterns into representations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of TPAD. Implementation codes are available at https://github.com/TiliaceaeSU/TPAD .

candidates.title: OWLET: On-Policy Weighted Learning via Evidence Transfer for Video Large Language Model Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Post-training has become a key stage for eliciting reasoning capabilities in Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs). Existing post-training methods mainly follow two paradigms: reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). However, they do not fully exploit visual evidence for effective training. RL supervises the policy with a single trajectory-level reward, which is too coarse-grained for video reasoning: the same response-level advantage is applied to every generated token, disregarding that the tokens of a video response are grounded in the visual stream to very different degrees. OPD provides token-level supervision through output-distribution matching, but lacks direct supervision of the spatiotemporal representations that produce those outputs. We observe across extensive experiments that the same model reasons more accurately when its video view combines global temporal context with question-relevant details. Comparing the same student-generated response under this view and uniform sampling reveals changes in token likelihoods and internal representations, providing a training signal for evidence use. Building on this observation, we propose OWLET, an evidence-privileged RL method that derives training signals from a richer teacher view. This view couples uniform global context with question-conditioned local windows, providing visual evidence without requiring a larger model. To better exploit this privileged visual evidence, OWLET introduces (i) \textbf{evidence-aware credit redistribution}, which compares token likelihoods across the two views and redistributes positive response-level advantages according to their relative evidence support; and (ii) \textbf{spatiotemporal state alignment}, which aligns the two views' hidden states on verifier-accepted responses.

candidates.title: A Survey on Post-Training of Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: The technical evolution of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has profoundly influenced the AI community, reshaping how intelligent systems understand, reason, and interact in both the digital and physical worlds. Through large-scale multimodal pretraining, MLLMs lay the foundation for general perception and alignment, while it remains unclear how such models can be transformed into human-grounded behaviors. Multimodal Post-Training, which further refines pretrained MLLMs to align their behaviors with human intent and real-world task demands, has become an important paradigm for advancing multimodal intelligence. Accordingly, both academia and industry have devoted increasing efforts to this direction, pushing the boundaries of multimodal general intelligence at an unprecedented pace. In this survey, we systematically review existing MMPoT research from a behavior-shaping perspective. Guided by this view, we introduce a unified framework that organizes existing MLLMs post-training methods into five major families: instruction following, preference calibration, reasoning enhancement, domain adaptation, and scalable learning. Moreover, we revisit benchmarks and evaluation protocols to critically assess the capabilities and limitations of post-trained MLLMs. To conclude, we provide a synthesized outlook on broader open questions, and highlight future research directions toward more general and reliable multimodal capabilities. An updated paper list is available at: https://github.com/zchoi/Awesome-post-training-for-MLLMs.

candidates.title: Performance of Consumer Multimodal Large Language Model Interfaces on a Selected Publication-derived Challenge Set of Initially Misdiagnosed Dermatologic Emergencies
candidates.abstract: Aim: To evaluate the diagnostic and safety-related response performance of consumer multimodal large language model interfaces on a selected publication-derived challenge set of initially misdiagnosed dermatologic emergencies. Materials and Methods:This exploratory cross-sectional study evaluated 50 cases of initially misdiagnosed dermatologic emergencies, selected from published reports identified between May 1 and June 1, 2026.ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude were tested on June 2, 2026, under text-only and text-plus-image conditions using a single standardized prompt.Outcomes were Top-1 and cumulative Top-4 accuracies, clinically appropriate emergency management, risk-triage failure, and harmful recommendations.Results: Top-1 accuracy ranged from 32.0% to 50.0% with text-only input and from 36.0% to 58.0% with text-plus-image input; corresponding Top-4 ranges were 50.0%-66.0%and 56.0%-74.0%.Appropriate management ranged from 38.0% to 54.0% and from 44.0% to 64.0%.No within-platform input-mode comparisons remained significant after Holm correction.Between-platform differences remained significant for Top-1 accuracy under both input conditions and for Top-4 accuracy and management appropriateness under text-plus-image input.Post-hoc differences primarily reflected lower observed performance for Claude than for Gemini in this dataset.Appropriate management occurred in 100% of Top-1-correct responses compared with 9.9% of Top-1-incorrect responses, whereas 18.0% of Top-4-correct responses had inappropriate management.Conclusion: Within this selected challenge set and a single standardized prompting condition, the platforms demonstrated moderate diagnostic performance and variable performance on safety-related responses.Correct Top-1 diagnosis closely corresponded to appropriate management, whereas Top-4 recognition did not ensure safe management.The findings represent a single-run technical benchmark and do not establish output reproducibility, clinical usefulness, real-world safety, or stable platform superiority.

candidates.title: Hierarchical Reasoning Gates for Multimodal Large Language Models in Dental Image Interpretation: A Prompt-Level Protocol for Improving Accuracy
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have been used to support dental image interpretation, but performance may depend on prompt structure. We proposed Hierarchical Reasoning Gates (HRG), a prompt-level protocol organizing image interpretation into sequential stages with validation before progression. Forty anonymized panoramic radiographs of impacted mandibular molars were analyzed using three prompt architectures: P1, zero-shot natural language; P2, a five-step structured workflow followed by a final internal-validation checkpoint; and P3, HRG with 10 macro-stages and 35 procedural control blocks. Outputs were compared with expert radiology reference reports using five predefined variables. Mean Total Score was 3.52 ± 0.85, 3.58 ± 0.71, and 4.35 ± 0.74 for P1, P2, and P3, respectively; Full Accuracy was 10.0%, 5.0%, and 50.0%. Reports with errors in three or more variables occurred in 12.5%, 7.5%, and 0%, respectively. Only Apparent Anatomical Relationship differed significantly across prompts after Holm adjustment. Test–retest repeatability was high for several variables but lower for Apparent Anatomical Relationship in P3. HRG was associated with higher image-interpretation performance and fewer complex error patterns, although higher performance did not uniformly translate into greater repeatability. These findings support gated prompt design for controlling dependent steps in MLLM-based image analysis, while clinical use still requires expert supervision.

candidates.title: Agentic Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm. Their ability to communicate with us in our own language, and to reason about our world, has made them a favorite tool for writing, answering questions, and much more. Their answers already influence our decisions and our actions. What would happen if LLMs themselves could act in the world directly? What would happen if LLMs could interact with each other? Agentic LLMs combine the power of large language models with the ability to act in the real world. In this book we will discuss how agentic LLMs work, how they act, how they interact, and what this means for us, as users.

candidates.title: A Survey on Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer new approaches to overcoming the limitations of recommendation systems in representation, user modeling, and decision-making. Accordingly, recommendation systems are evolving from paradigms primarily based on behavioral statistics and discriminative learning toward new paradigms featuring semantic understanding, reasoning-based decision-making, and autonomous interaction. This paper systematically reviews recent advances in LLM-empowered recommendation systems. The principal advantages of LLMs in semantic modeling, knowledge transfer, and generative reasoning are analyzed. Then, the representative technical paradigms including representation-enhanced recommendation, user-interest and context enhancement, prompt learning and task reformulation, and generative recommendation are subsequently reviewed and summarized. Finally, the paper analyzes major challenges related to hallucination, inference efficiency, privacy and security, fairness and trustworthiness, and recommendation agents, and outlines future research directions.

candidates.title: Phonology-Aware Speaker Extraction Frontend for Audio LLMs
candidates.abstract: Target speaker extraction (TSE) is a key frontend for enabling audio large language models (LLMs) to recognize and understand a designated speaker in overlapping speech. However, multilingual mixtures exhibit heterogeneous extraction demands, causing fixed-depth systems to either under-process challenging inputs or waste computation on inputs that have already converged. Existing TSE frontends generally apply uniform computation, while Audio-LLM adaptation methods neither explicitly model language-conditioned extraction demands nor preserve plug-and-play compatibility with frozen downstream models. We therefore propose LATTE, a lightweight 5.2M-parameter frontend that combines an acoustic Difficulty Estimator, a task-adaptive phonology-informed prior learned from multi-depth TSE gains, and an Adaptive Hourglass Extractor to route each mixture without requiring language identity at inference. On PolyExtract, LATTE achieves a macro SI-SNRi of 15.07 dB at 0.30 GFLOPs, retaining performance within 0.09 dB of a 0.53-GFLOP fixed-depth model while reducing computation by 43.4%, and lowers the average WER from 16.8% to 14.6% relative to TF-GridNet. By jointly modeling sample-level extraction demands and phonological structure, LATTE provides a practical framework for quality-aware, compute-efficient multilingual TSE and offers a scalable path toward robust Audio-LLM deployment.

candidates.title: Projected Primal–Dual Gradient Preference Optimization Under Category-Wise Split-Conformal Safety Constraints for Large Language Model Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Preference optimisation improves helpfulness, but a single aggregate safety penalty lets frequent harm categories dominate the objective while rare ones bear the residual risk. This paper models post-training as a vector-constrained programme: the pairwise preference loss is minimised under one risk tolerance per harm category. The solver is a projected primal–dual gradient recursion that prices each category by its own residual violation. For a nonconvex objective we bound three horizon-averaged residuals—primal stationarity, dual regret and the average constraint value—for the unbiased, unclipped recursion and a uniformly drawn iterate; the implemented recursion is compared empirically with a no-EMA, no-clipping form of itself. Certification stays separate from optimisation: on an untouched calibration split, a multiplicity-adjusted fixed-sequence test gives release thresholds valid for all categories at once under correct category assignment, with an additive bound for learned routers. It certifies the scoring and filtering of corpus-distributed candidate responses, not text the trained policy generates. In one exploratory setting—one Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct backbone, PKU-SafeRLHF, three seeds—the recursion meets the per-category tolerance that direct preference optimisation and scalar-constrained schemes violate, cutting the worst-category miss rate at the training threshold from 0.176 to 0.057 at unchanged preference accuracy. The certified operating point barely moves: most of the constraint’s effect is a score translation shared by the harmful and benign responses of a prompt, which calibration provably absorbs. Whether a training constraint holds and whether the deployed gate is safer are different questions.

candidates.title: Systemic privacy risks of personal data exposure through conversational large language model agents
candidates.abstract: Abstract Conversational Large Language Model (LLM) agents, deployed quickly, have exposed unprecedented opportunities for personal information, from health data to financial information, to biometric identifiers. This critical enlightenment review investigates general privacy dangers in each of five areas: data leakage and memorization, adversarial extraction and prompt injection, inference and re-identification, surveillance and profiling and regulatory governance breakdown. We trace privacy threats from static data breaches to dynamic ones that have become part of an architecture, associated with neural memorization and contextual inference (2020–2026), using expert selection of primary studies and technical benchmark sources. Upon close examination, technical mitigations (differential privacy, federated learning and machine unlearning) prove successful to some extent when operating in controlled environments, but fail to provide complete protection in conversational environments. We combine classical theory on Privacy-Preserving Data Publishing (PPDP) with emerging threats from LLMs, and present a conflict-of-evidence analysis which reveals that privacy protections are particularly effective in structured environments with low risks, or with consumers actively responsible for maintaining them, but fail to adequately protect privacy in high-stakes domains without human control, technical safeguards, and legal liability. We systematically examine and analyze a dimension that has not been studied sufficiently: risks of data deletion and editing illusion, and introduce techniques for unlearning machines that leave behind traces that can be exploited by adversarial reconstruction. We support the multi-layered mitigation framework of PPDP principles, technical safeguards, and governance reform.

candidates.title: Emergence of polarization in networks of large language model agents
candidates.abstract: Abstract Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have empowered autonomous agents to generate social networks, communicate, and form shared and diverging opinions on political issues. However, our understanding of their collective behaviours and underlying mechanisms remains incomplete. In this paper, we simulate networked systems involving thousands of LLM agents across different backbone models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, ChatGLM, Llama-3, and DeepSeek-V3), in which agents interact through LLM-guided conversations and update their opinions over time, resulting in the emergence of opinion polarization. We discover that these agents spontaneously develop their own social network with properties characteristic of human social networks, such as homophilic clustering. The collective opinions of these LLM agents evolve in ways that exhibit behavioural patterns consistent with social phenomena and mechanisms widely discussed in empirical studies of human behaviour and opinion-dynamics models. This consistency suggests that LLM agents can serve as a valuable synthetic testbed for exploring hypothetical intervention strategies in networked LLM-agent systems. Using this testbed, we further examine the effects of a range of network- and individual-level interventions, such as promoting more diverse interactions and reducing confirmation bias. Overall, this work not only sheds light on subtle opinion dynamics and collective behaviour of LLM agents from a network perspective, but also demonstrates their potential for testing hypotheses about opinion dynamics and intervention strategies.

candidates.title: Evaluating Local Language Model Agents for Reproducible Data Engineering: An Empirical Software Engineering Study of Mobility Workflows
candidates.abstract: Context: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as software and data-engineering assistants, yet evidence about locally deployable open-weight agents remains limited. Existing evaluations often emphasize textual responses or isolated code generation rather than the validity of complete engineering artifacts. Objectives: We evaluate whether local LLM agents can produce correct and reproducible data-engineering artifacts, quantify the effect of a closed-loop workspace condition, and examine trade-offs in model scale, architecture, quantization, runtime, tool use, and failure. Methods: We introduce a benchmark of fifteen mobility-workflow tasks covering data discovery, connectors, transport-feed processing, semantic enrichment, feature engineering, validation, visualization, and reporting. Deterministic checkers assess generated scripts, tables, structured files, figures, and reports. Ten local configurations are evaluated in one-shot and closed-loop conditions, with five repetitions per model, mode, and task, yielding 1,500 scored attempts on a consumer-grade GPU. Results: Among models larger than two billion parameters, the workspace condition increases pass rates by 26.7-52.0 percentage points over one-shot generation. The strongest configuration reaches 85.3% artifact-level success, and a quantized 9-billion-parameter model reaches 69.3% with an approximately 6.5 GB memory footprint. Gains are largest when intermediate artifacts expose errors the agent can inspect and repair. Conclusion: Local open-weight agents can support a meaningful subset of software-intensive data-engineering work, but reliability depends on model capability, task verifiability, and deterministic validation. The benchmark provides a reproducible method for evaluating complete agent configurations before adoption in engineering workflows.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Applications and Development in the Field of Electronic Test Instruments
candidates.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), especially the fast iteration and widespread deployment of large language models (LLMs), has ushered in a new paradigm for the intelligent augmentation of electronic test instruments and automatic test systems (ATS). By combining the powerful reasoning and generative capabilities of LLMs with the timeliness and accuracy of external knowledge bases, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a highly promising approach to addressing knowledge-intensive challenges in the operation and maintenance of electronic test instruments. This paper presents a comprehensive review of RAG and its applications in the field of electronic test instruments. First, the basic architecture of RAG is reviewed, including retrieval mechanisms, knowledge-base construction, and generative models. Then, considering the operational characteristics of electronic test instruments and automatic test systems, key knowledge-intensive tasks are analyzed, such as fault diagnosis, test configuration, and process planning, followed by a discussion of representative RAG-based applications, including intelligent fault diagnosis systems, adaptive test-parameter configuration, and interactive question-answering assistants. In addition, practical considerations for engineering implementation are discussed with respect to knowledge-base construction and effectiveness evaluation. Finally, open issues and future research directions are outlined, including multimodal RAG, federated learning for distributed knowledge bases, and edge deployment. This review aims to provide researchers and practitioners in relevant industries with a comprehensive understanding of the current status and development prospects of RAG technologies in electronic test instruments.

candidates.title: A Security Meta-Model for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems extend large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge through a multi-stage pipeline. While this architecture can improve the factual grounding of generated answers, it introduces structural attack surfaces that extend beyond those of standalone LLMs. In this paper, we introduce a security meta-model that captures explicit causal relationships between RAG surfaces, attacks, weaknesses, risks, and CIA impact (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability). Its purpose is to provide security engineers with a structured and user-friendly framework for gathering and assessing the risks, weaknesses, and mitigations relevant to their RAG deployment. We designed the meta-model through an iterative, structured analysis of 43~publications (2023--2026) and instantiated it as a catalog populated with the security threats and remediations reported in the literature. Filtering the catalog according to a deployment configuration produces a risk profile containing the risks applicable to that deployment. An interactive web visualizer lets users navigate the catalog as a graph, follow causal chains, and explore stakeholder-specific views. Analysis of the catalog revealed a persistent imbalance between attack-focused and defense-focused research, a concentration of threats at ingestion, and coverage gaps affecting output integrity. Coverage is assessed against the OWASP LLM Top~10, and operational applicability is illustrated across textual, graph-based, and multimodal RAG configurations.

candidates.title: Rethinking Contrastive Loss in CLIP Post-training: A Complementary Framework with Frozen Text Encoder
candidates.abstract: CLIP serves as a foundational vision-language model and the de facto vision encoder for downstream VLMs such as LLaVA. Post-training offers a lightweight route to refine CLIP, but recent work argues that the standard contrastive loss is unsuitable for post-training due to catastrophic forgetting under small batches, motivating designs that abandon the contrastive objective in favor of distillation. We revisit this premise and find that, for the InfoNCE objective, the reported forgetting is driven primarily not by insufficient negatives but by an inappropriate magnitude of the contrastive temperature $τ$: with $τ$ set sufficiently small, contrastive post-training improves rather than degrades the pretrained CLIP, which we explain through the temperature dependence of the InfoNCE gradient. Building on this finding, we propose \textbf{ComCLIP}, a lightweight single-epoch post-training recipe that freezes CLIP's text encoder---so the refined vision encoder is a drop-in replacement with unchanged architecture and inference cost---and trains the vision encoder with a properly-tempered contrastive loss, an MSE anchoring loss against the original CLIP, and a relational distillation loss from DINOv2. Over multiple seeds, ComCLIP matches the self-distillation baseline CLIP-Refine on zero-shot classification while significantly improving the transferability of visual features, measured by linear probing ($48.99$ vs.\ $42.28$ on ViT-B/16), and on ViT-L/14 it also improves MMVP over CLIP-Refine ($24.20$ vs.\ $19.01$); CLIP-Refine remains stronger on image-text retrieval. Used as a drop-in vision encoder for LLaVA-1.5-7B without re-aligning the projector or LLM, ComCLIP yields no net change across $8$ VLM benchmarks, i.e., the refinement does not break downstream compatibility. Code and models are available at https://github.com/showstarpro/ComCLIP.git.

candidates.title: RAG-Stress: Probing the Limits of Evidence Reliance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Following retrieved evidence does not guarantee factual correctness: misleading evidence can induce a model to replace an answer it previously gave correctly. Standard accuracy measures obscure this behavior by combining answer replacement with preexisting errors. We introduce RAG-Stress, a controlled diagnostic protocol for examining the limits of evidence reliance in retrieval-augmented generation. The protocol holds the question and reference answer fixed, edits one assertion to support a designated incorrect answer, and crosses two source priority policies with three positions of the answer span within the evidence text. We measure misleading rate (MR) on each model's subset of questions answered correctly without retrieval, alongside clean accuracy on the full evaluation set. We evaluate fifteen systems spanning API models, open models, and search agents trained with reinforcement learning on TriviaQA-RC, HotpotQA, and SearchQA, with additional English and Chinese MedQA evaluations. Instructions that prioritize documents consistently produce higher MR than those permitting reliance on prior knowledge. Averaged over models and positions, the gap ranges from 10.9 to 13.5 percentage points across the three QA datasets. Mean MR follows End $>$ Beginning $>$ Middle under both policies, although individual models do not uniformly follow this ordering. A separate paired audit of 500 questions and two checkpoints supports increased harmful override without establishing a corresponding improvement in beneficial correction. These findings distinguish evidence adherence from factual reliability and motivate evaluating whether retrieved evidence preserves, replaces, or corrects a model's answers.

candidates.title: RAGenome: Scaling Retrieval-Based Genomic Language Models to Long Contexts
candidates.abstract: The genome holds the blueprint that governs the biological properties of the cell. Consequently, advancing our knowledge of genomic function is crucial both for a broader understanding of biology and for continued biomedical advances. The success of large language models on natural language and protein sequences has motivated similar efforts on genomic data. However, standard genomic language models (gLMs) often require extremely large computational resources and still fall behind traditional methods on some downstream tasks. Recently, MSA-based pretraining has been proposed as an efficient alternative, but existing models are limited to short input contexts, restricting their use to short-range tasks, such as variant effect prediction. In this work, we present RAGenome, the first retrieval-based gLM that scales pretraining to longer contexts (100$\times$ longer than existing MSA-based gLMs), allowing it to capture both across-species evolutionary relationships and within-species longer-range interactions. Trained on whole-genome alignments from 100 vertebrates, RAGenome substantially improves the long-range capabilities of MSA-based gLMs, raising gene finding performance from 0.45 to 0.60, while remaining competitive on purely evolutionary-based tasks like prioritizing pathogenic variants. RAGenome provides competitive gLM performance at a fraction of the training cost, unifying evolutionary modeling and long-range capabilities within a single, flexible, scalable framework. Code is available at https://github.com/PanosAntoniadis/RAGenome.

candidates.title: Large language models unlock the ecology of species interactions
candidates.abstract: Species interactions shape population dynamics, geographic distributions, evolutionary trajectories, and responses to environmental change. Yet data on these interactions remain scarce across broad spatial, temporal, and taxonomic scales because they are difficult to collect in the field. One promising source of interaction data is citizen science platforms, which contain billions of biodiversity observations, often accompanied by unstructured text comments that may document interactions among organisms. Advances in large language models (LLMs) make it increasingly feasible to identify, extract, and categorize biotic interactions from these unstructured data at scale. Here, we present an LLM workflow that collects species interaction observations from multilingual citizen science comments. Using two case studies-bird-bird and plant-pollinator interactions-we show that LLMs can rapidly extract interaction types and participating species with high accuracy. These data can greatly expand the spatial, temporal, and taxonomic coverage and resolution of species interactions data, enable new tests of long-standing ecological questions, and improve our ability to track ecological changes. With appropriate validation, expert review, and attention to data privacy for both users and sensitive species, this approach opens new opportunities to characterize, forecast, and conserve biodiversity under global change.

I argue that these technologies expand the scale, methodological range, and scope for delegation, while the basic logic by which those measurements support cultural claims remains mostly unchanged.

candidates.title: Incremental Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Human-in-the-Loop Decision Support
candidates.abstract: We introduce iRAG, a human-in-the-loop decision-support system combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Hybrid Decision-Making. Unlike conventional RAG systems, relying on static Knowledge Bases (KBs), our proposal addresses settings where the KB is initially empty and is progressively populated through human decisions. The system stores previous decisions as retrievable precedents and moves from silent observation to evidence-grounded contestation and, finally, to autonomous handling with abstention. Against an independent baseline, iRAG matches final-decision error under 10% drift without retrieval decay and reduces it under 40% drift across all configurations. Retrieval decay improves performance on changed knowledge while increasing error on stable knowledge, evidencing a stability--plasticity trade-off rather than a general advantage. Human oversight is an architectural provision of the workflow; its usability with real human users remains to be evaluated.
